title: DCS — Discite Computatrum Scientia
subtitle: Computer science education that doesn't need a computer.

sections.heading: Current Status
sections.content: The course is written and reviewed; the storytelling phase is underway. All 18 lessons of the DCS Programming Course are complete — 54 documents in total, a lesson plan, a teacher guide, and a student handout for each — and every lesson now opens with a story from the Farmer Joe universe: a wacky farm where precise instructions, a bossy wife at the window, and a very literal cow carry the computer science. The canon map behind those stories passed an independent correctness review — zero wrong computer science found, and the reviewer's fixes are folded in. Next up: standalone concept-stories learners can retell at home, teacher training, and mechanical computing devices.

sections.heading: The Why
sections.content: There are millions of children in rural communities with little or no technology access who will never touch a computer in a classroom. But computational thinking — decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithms — doesn't need a screen. It needs a teacher who knows how to play the right games. DCS is a curriculum of unplugged activities: board games, card games, group challenges, storytelling, and physical movement. No computers required, every concept sticks. Because these learners aren't being prepared to survive the digital world as passive consumers — they're being prepared to shape it as innovators and problem solvers.

sections.heading: The Vision
sections.content: Years ago I wrote that every child should learn computer science, not to become a programmer, but to become a creator — someone who understands the logic behind the tools they use, rather than just consuming whatever tech hands them. That philosophy hasn't aged a day. DCS is the practical manifestation of that idea: a full lesson plan series built for the reality of rural classrooms where a teacher's creativity matters more than a computer lab budget. Revived in 2026 with a sharper scope: two pillars — computational thinking (decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithms) and programming as a mindset, taught without a single computer — for middle school through high school, in classrooms where the only technology is a teacher's creativity. The world these learners are growing into is increasingly digital; the point is that they meet it as innovators and problem solvers, not as passive consumers.

sections.heading: What's Next
sections.content: The course skeleton is done — now it gets its stories. The Farmer Joe universe grows into a standalone series of concept-stories: cute, enduring stories that teach the CS ideas and go home with the learners. Then teacher training, so a teacher with no tech background can walk in and run a lesson with chalk, stones, and bottle caps. And further out, a small canon of mechanical computing devices from history — abacus, slide rule, stepped drums — buildable, affordable, and no electricity required.
